title: The Quantum Endgame Is Not About Cleaner Qubits, It's About Who Can Mass-Produce on a Phone-Chip Line
dek: The quantum endgame is not about whose qubits are cleaner, but about who can mass-produce using existing semiconductor fabs; silicon spin qubits reuse TSMC lithography, while ion traps are stuck at a hundred thousand laser beams and superconductors at warehouse-sized refrigerators.
why: The exclusive value is in the second half: HRL paper's CNOT error rate, AI auto-tuning, and FFP's striking scores; the first half's principle explanations are more introductory, and veterans can fast-forward.
who: Investors focused on quantum computing route selection, semiconductor process engineers, and security practitioners wanting to calibrate the quantum decryption timeline.
skip: Listeners already familiar with superconducting and ion trap principles can skip from 57:56 to 1:28:00.

points.h: Ion traps and superconductors need miracles first; silicon doesn't
points.body: To build an ion trap with a hundred thousand qubits, you'd first need to invent the optical miracle of a hundred thousand laser beams; for a million superconducting qubits, you'd need a cryostat the size of a warehouse; for a million spin qubits, you just run a standard 300mm silicon wafer through the same lithography equipment that TSMC, ASML, and Intel use to make phone processors. Krishna uses this to set the tone for the whole episode: the key to the quantum race is not single-qubit fidelity, but whether the path to scaling already exists within the industrial system.

points.h: Quantum computing is no longer about principles, but engineering
points.body: In 2000, DiVincenzo proposed five criteria, aiming to dismiss liquid-state NMR quantum computing. This episode of FFP proposes its own three criteria: qubit quality, control, and scalability with economics. The rest of the episode scores four routes—superconducting, ion trap, neutral atom, and silicon spin—item by item. Laying out the evaluation framework itself tells you: quantum computing has entered the stage of engineering competition, and you can't just talk about principles.

points.h: Superconducting isn't a technical failure, it's an engineering impossibility
points.body: Estimates show that a thousand logical qubits require ten million transmon physical qubits. Control line count is limited by the cooling capacity of dilution refrigerators, frequencies are crowded, and helium-3 supply becomes a new resource constraint. FFP gives superconducting only 1/10 on scalability and economics, with a total score of 11/30. This is the first time the show separates 'technically strong' from 'engineering infeasible'—a warehouse-sized refrigerator means even data centers might not fit it.

points.h: Ion traps win on coherence time, lose on gate speed
points.body: Ion traps have coherence times up to ten hours, but gate operations rely on phonons and are limited by the Paul trap oscillation frequency, making them about a thousand times slower than superconducting. The result is counterintuitive: even if ion traps could scale to break encryption, cracking 2048-bit RSA would take about a year, while superconducting would take about eight hours. Long coherence time does not mean more work per unit time; for practical computing, slow gate time is a throughput disaster.

points.h: The quantum threat is neither tomorrow nor never
points.body: A March 2026 paper from Harvard, Caltech, and Qera says ten thousand qubits might break internet encryption, but it would actually take years; even with a hundred thousand physical qubits, under mathematically optimal assumptions, breaking RSA would take about three months. This figure strikes both extreme narratives: the quantum threat is not tomorrow, but it is certainly not forever distant. To achieve 'breakable in months', you need qubit count, gate speed, and error correction all to meet the bar simultaneously.

points.h: Quantum companies live or die by government contracts
points.body: HRL lost key project funding in early 2026 and laid off 376 people. Government funding shifted from basic research to applied research demanding rapid commercialization; IBM and Intel received support from the CHIPS Act, and ultimately IBM acquired HRL. Krishna calls this the debut of quantum computing's MVP: quantum companies' fates hinge on government contracts, and being acquired is not a failure but a way for the technology to enter an industrial system with manufacturing capability.

points.h: A million qubits can't be tuned by hand; it's image recognition now
points.body: Automated tuning becomes key to scaling: a 2023 paper could tune six electrons by hand, but manual tuning of a million qubits would take a human lifetime. Tuning is essentially image recognition—when scanning voltage, tunneling events appear as stripes, and Krishna's team uses DETR combined with ResNet and Transformer to automatically recognize stripes and generate parameters. This is also the hidden premise for why silicon spin can reuse semiconductor fabs: no matter how many qubits, software can auto-align them.

points.h: Silicon may not be first, but it will be the last winner
points.body: FFP's final scores: silicon spin gets 10/10 on qubit quality, 10/10 on control (provided isotope enrichment and valley state issues are solved), and 10000/10 on scalability and economics, for a total of 10020/30; neutral atoms score negative 3000. Krishna admits silicon may not be the first route to achieve fault tolerance, but once it does, it will become the final standard because it is cheap and manufacturable, just as transistors replaced vacuum tubes.
